entries.clue: Chorister's ablution with regular purging (4)

indicators.note: Regular picks out the letters that fall at even steps through a word, and purging throws that set away.

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters of the word, read in order

annotation.surface: A choir singer at the washbasin, scrubbing away thoroughly before the service.
annotation.walkthrough: Regular is the crossword's word for every second letter, and purging them leaves the odd ones standing. The washing image is there so that 'ablution' looks like meaning rather than raw material.
annotation.definitionFit: Chorister → ALTO: the alto is the choir's second-highest voice and the singer who takes that line, so the definition names one by example.

entries.clue: Chairperson suppressing pride? (4,5)

blocks.note: the surface offers whoever runs the meeting; the setter means somebody holding a chair out in front of them, legs first, as a tool of the trade
pride is vanity on the surface, and also the collective noun for a family of big cats, which is the one that has to be kept down

annotation.surface: A committee chair keeping their own vanity firmly in check during a meeting.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman's question mark is the only signal that both halves have swapped worlds at once: the chair is furniture rather than office, and the pride pads about on four legs. The whip is optional; the chair is traditional.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines the job: a person who faces a pride of big cats with a chair in one hand and keeps them under control.

entries.clue: Cavort around, 'entertaining' Everyman's beginning to ham it up (7)

indicators.note: Anything sent around ends up somewhere other than where it started, and letters sent around end up out of their order.
To entertain a guest is to take them into the house, so the letter alongside is taken into the mix rather than left outside it.

blocks.note: six letters of fodder
Everyman is the setter's own name, and its beginning is the letter it opens with

annotation.surface: Everyman capering about the stage and playing host from the very first moment.
annotation.walkthrough: Everyman signs his clues most weeks, and here his initial is the seventh letter the shuffle needs. The quotation marks round 'entertaining' are the setter admitting that the word has a job to do beyond describing the fun.
annotation.definitionFit: ham it up → OVERACT: both mean pushing a performance well past what the part needs, the actor playing to the back row and beyond.

entries.clue: Last two pieces missing from puzzle depicting lively dances (4)

indicators.note: A piece of a word is a letter, and the two at the end are the ones that have gone astray.

blocks.note: the picture puzzle you tip out of a box and fit back together, with its last two letters then taken off

annotation.surface: A half-finished puzzle whose picture shows people dancing, two of its pieces lost.
annotation.walkthrough: The word 'pieces' belongs to the picture on the table and to the letters at once, which is why nothing in the sentence looks like an instruction. Only one kind of puzzle comes in pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: lively dances → JIGS: the fast hopping dance of Irish and Scottish tradition, played in six-eight time, so the plural is a set of them.

entries.clue: Judge unwise: unripe berry used in booze (7)

indicators.note: An unwise head is a muddled one, and muddled is how the letters standing next to the word arrive.

blocks.note: J is the short form law reports use for a judge
six letters shaken into a different order

annotation.surface: A magistrate called foolish for saying a green berry is fit for the still.
annotation.walkthrough: Juniper berries are what make gin taste of gin, so 'booze' is precise rather than vague. 'Unwise' sits directly beside its fodder, which is where an anagram indicator has to be if the clue is to be fair.
annotation.definitionFit: berry used in booze → JUNIPER: its blue-black berries are the flavouring that makes gin gin, so the shrub is named by what its fruit is for.

entries.clue: Blast! Zero enthusiasm (5)

blocks.note: a blast of wind is a gust of it
nothing written as a circle

annotation.surface: Someone swearing mildly at a complete absence of keenness in the room.
annotation.walkthrough: The exclamation mark turns 'Blast!' into an oath, which is exactly what hides the weather sense the wordplay wants. Zero as O is one of the first conventions worth owning outright.
annotation.definitionFit: enthusiasm → GUSTO: doing a thing with gusto is doing it with relish and appetite, the same eagerness the noun names.

entries.clue: Assuming 'geriatrics' enfeebled, I'm seldom tolerant, primarily? (6)

definitions.text: Assuming 'geriatrics' enfeebled, I'm seldom tolerant, primarily?

indicators.note: Primarily asks for what comes first, so every word in the sentence gives up only the letter it opens with.

blocks.note: the opening letters of the three words, taken in order
the same treatment applied to the next three words

annotation.surface: Somebody owning up to running out of patience with old people rather quickly.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Primarily' waits until the end of the sentence and then governs every word in it. The quotation marks round 'geriatrics' are the setter standing back from a word only the speaker would use.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight the whole clue is a confession: a person who assumes the old are feeble and shows them little patience is precisely what the word names.

entries.clue: Smiley perhaps pulling in gut, short and stout (6)

indicators.note: To pull something in is to draw it inside you, so the letters it governs sit in the middle rather than alongside.

blocks.note: George Smiley, the mole-hunter of John le Carre's novels, works in British intelligence, and 'perhaps' flags him as one example
tum is the nursery word for the stomach

annotation.surface: A man breathing in to look trimmer, described all the same as short and stout.
annotation.walkthrough: The surname does the misdirecting: read as a description it means cheerful, and it belongs to le Carre's spymaster. 'Short and stout' is one definition in four words, not two definitions joined by 'and'.
annotation.definitionFit: short and stout → STUMPY: the word for something squat, low to the ground and thick with it, so both halves of the definition land on the one adjective.

entries.clue: Cause aggravation - by rustling? (3,8,4)

blocks.note: the idiom for needling a person until they lose their temper
rustling is the theft of livestock off a farm, the cattle-thief's trade

annotation.surface: A question about whether stealing livestock is a reliable way to annoy people.
annotation.walkthrough: The idiom is said to come from the racing stable, where a nervous thoroughbred was calmed by a goat kept in its stall and rivals stole the goat the night before a race. Rustling makes the phrase literal.
annotation.definitionFit: Cause aggravation → GET SOMEONE'S GOAT: the idiom for irritating a person past patience, while the same words read literally describe taking a goat that belongs to somebody else.

entries.clue: Heroic text's adapted as scary film (3,8)

indicators.note: A text adapted for the screen is rewritten rather than reprinted, and letters adapted are reset in a new order.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder, the apostrophe-s handing over its S

annotation.surface: A brave book being turned into a horror film for the cinema.
annotation.walkthrough: The apostrophe repays a second look: it reads as a contraction of 'text is' and quietly supplies a letter. The film really was an adaptation, of William Peter Blatty's novel, which is why 'adapted' sits so innocently in the sentence.
annotation.definitionFit: scary film → THE EXORCIST: the 1973 possession picture that spent decades as the byword for the most frightening film ever released, so the definition names it by example.

entries.clue: Funny one I loved in YouTube clip? (6,5)

indicators.note: Funny means out of true as well as amusing, and letters out of true are letters out of order.

blocks.note: eleven letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Somebody recalling an amusing appearance by a person they were once fond of.
annotation.walkthrough: The shuffling instruction is the very first word, which is where a solver least expects it. The question mark is the setter conceding that the definition is one instance of the answer rather than a synonym for it.
annotation.definitionFit: YouTube clip? → ONLINE VIDEO: a clip on YouTube is one kind of video watched over the internet, so the definition works by example, as the question mark admits.

entries.clue: Drink in a deceit, haplessly (4,3)

indicators.note: A hapless act is a clumsy, unlucky one, and letters put down haplessly do not land in the order they were given.

blocks.note: seven letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Somebody swallowing a lie whole, and coming off badly for it.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Drink in' looks like a single phrase — to drink in a scene is to enjoy it — and the join runs straight between the two words. 'In' is joinery here, not an instruction to put anything inside anything.
annotation.definitionFit: Drink → ICED TEA: the chilled brew sold by the bottle and the jug, a drink named by example rather than by synonym.

entries.clue: Copper to steal from the French museum's entrance? A concern (7)

indicators.note: A building's entrance is the way in at the front of it, and a word's entrance is the letter it comes in by.

blocks.note: a copper is a penny, and p is how the coin is written
to rob is to steal
'the' in French is le
the first letter of the word, the one standing at its entrance

annotation.surface: A policeman lifting something from just inside the door of a French museum.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Copper' wants very badly to be the policeman the surface is about, and it is the coin in your pocket. Four separate scraps build the answer, which is why no single word of the wordplay looks like wordplay.
annotation.definitionFit: A concern → PROBLEM: a thing that worries you and wants solving; the two nouns swap into each other in any sentence.

entries.clue: Extra time, erroneously, in cabbie's device (9)

indicators.note: Something done erroneously is done wrong, and letters set down wrong are letters no longer in their proper order.

blocks.note: nine letters of fodder

annotation.surface: Added minutes credited by mistake on a taxi driver's machine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Extra time' arrives as a football phrase, and the football is the whole disguise. The device meant is the one ticking on a cab's dashboard while the fare climbs.
annotation.definitionFit: cabbie's device → TAXIMETER: the dashboard machine that measures the fare as a cab runs, and the instrument the word taxi was shortened from.

entries.clue: Passed quickly - for feedback? (3,2)

definitions.note: The second definition is elliptical: you run a thing by somebody for feedback, so the phrase carries that sense in context rather than equalling the words on its own.

blocks.note: what a runner does going past you on the towpath
the office idiom: you put an idea to a colleague to see what they make of it

annotation.surface: Something went past at a sprint, apparently so that comments could be invited.
annotation.walkthrough: Both halves need the same two short words, and the second is the phrase heard in every office — run it by me — put into the past. The dash does the job a definition-splitting comma usually does.
annotation.definitionFit: Passed quickly → RAN BY: to run by is to go past at speed, while running a thing by someone puts it to them for an opinion.

entries.clue: Pondered what lake's surface may have done (9)

definitions.text: what lake's surface may have done

blocks.note: turned a thing over in the mind, and at length

blocks.clueFragment: what lake's surface may have done
blocks.note: still water throws the image of the sky and the trees straight back at you

annotation.surface: Somebody thinking hard about what the surface of a lake has been up to.
annotation.walkthrough: There is a pond sitting inside 'pondered', which is Everyman's joke and not his wordplay — no letter of the clue is ever touched. Both halves are past tense, which is what makes the swap exact.
annotation.definitionFit: Pondered → REFLECTED: to reflect is to think a matter over, and water reflects when it throws back the image of whatever stands above it.

entries.clue: Doctor who may be a smoker (5)

blocks.note: the one whose business is making a sick person well again
the trade that hangs bacon and herring over a smouldering fire to keep them

annotation.surface: A physician who might well be found outside with a cigarette.
annotation.walkthrough: The smoker in the surface has a cigarette; the one the setter means has a shed full of kippers. 'May be' is the warning that the second half names one branch of the trade rather than all of it.
annotation.definitionFit: Doctor → CURER: one who cures — illness in the first half of the clue, and bacon, ham or fish in the second, where curing is done with smoke.

entries.clue: Apprehended and, where hearings take place, heard (6)

indicators.note: Heard puts the test in the ear, so the match the clue wants is between two noises and not two spellings.

blocks.note: hearings are held in a court, and an English speaker sounds that word with no r in it at all

annotation.surface: Somebody arrested, and given a hearing in the place hearings happen.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue sets 'hearings' right beside 'heard' so that one word looks like part of the other's business. English that drops its r is what lets a courtroom and an arrest share a single noise.
annotation.definitionFit: Apprehended → CAUGHT: the everyday past tense of catching a person, which is exactly what an arrest amounts to.

entries.clue: Slap-happy greetings? (4-5)

definitions.note: 'Slap-happy' is an adjective and the answer a plural noun: Everyman is using the hyphenated word for its two halves, slaps given in delight, rather than for its dictionary sense of punch-drunk.

blocks.note: take the hyphen at its word: a blow of the open palm, delivered out of sheer pleasure
what two people exchange on meeting, here without a word being spoken

annotation.surface: Hellos from people cheerful enough to be called slap-happy about it.
annotation.walkthrough: The dictionary's slap-happy means dazed from too many blows to the head, which is the reading the hyphen invites and the wrong one here. Everyman wants the two words prised apart: the slap, and the delight in it.
annotation.definitionFit: greetings → HIGH-FIVES: palms smacked together overhead as a hello, which makes each one a slap given in delight — both halves of the clue at once.

entries.clue: Voodoo Child rocker Jimi ultimately bearing number that's entertained? (7)

definitions.text: Voodoo Child rocker Jimi ultimately bearing number that's entertained?

indicators.note: Ultimately points at the end of a thing, so each word in the run hands over only its final letter.
A bearer carries its load on top of itself, so what is borne sits above the letters bearing it as the answer runs down the grid.
To entertain somebody is to have them inside your house, so these letters are kept within the word beside them.

blocks.note: a hex is a spell put on somebody, which is what voodoo deals in, and it opens to let the rest in
n is the mathematician's stand-in for a number
the last letter of each of the three words, taken in order

annotation.surface: A guitarist on stage, ending with a number the crowd is enjoying.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Voodoo' works twice over: it names the song in the title and supplies the three letters that wrap everything else. The words handing over their tails are the same ones naming the man, which is why the sentence reads straight the whole way through.
annotation.definitionFit: Read straight, the whole clue describes the man: the rocker behind Voodoo Child, Jimi, playing a number that entertains — and the same words spell him out.

entries.clue: Artificial intelligence, mostly Grok for example, rising in former Soviet state (7)

indicators.note: Mostly is all but the last scrap, so the word hands over everything except the letter it ends on.
A down answer runs from the top of the grid downwards, so anything rising in it is read from the bottom up, back to front.

blocks.note: the two initials the technology is universally known by
Grok is one of the chatbots, and most of the name is it less its final letter
eg is the short form of exempli gratia, the standard way of saying 'for example'

annotation.surface: The newest chatbot, Grok say, catching on fast in a country that was once Soviet.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grok for example' is a second helping of the idea the clue opened with, which is what makes the two pieces look like one phrase. Down clues rise rather than reverse — there is no backwards on a vertical axis.
annotation.definitionFit: former Soviet state → GEORGIA: the republic in the Caucasus that left the USSR in 1991, not the American state that shares the name.

entries.clue: Appeared to be what you can do on Riviera (6)

blocks.note: what your eyes let you do when there is a view in front of them
the Med is what the British call the Mediterranean, the sea that coast looks out over

annotation.surface: Somebody describing the one activity a holiday on the Riviera guarantees you.
annotation.walkthrough: The wordplay is a small sentence rather than a pair of synonyms: stand on that coast and what you can do is see the Med. Holidaymakers have called the Mediterranean the Med for generations.
annotation.definitionFit: Appeared to be → SEEMED: the past tense of seem, which is what a thing does when it looks a certain way without any promise of being it.

entries.clue: Something tells you I'm not a horse, and that's the point (7)

definitions.text: Something tells you I'm not a horse, and that's the point

blocks.clueFragment: Something tells you I'm not a horse
blocks.note: the beast itself is speaking, and what gives it away is the single feature no horse has ever grown
two senses in four words: the sharp spiral thing on its forehead, and the whole point the setter is making

annotation.surface: An animal insisting, politely and in the first person, that it is not a horse.
annotation.walkthrough: The clue is the answer talking about itself, and 'the point' is the evidence and the joke at once. Everything else about the creature is a white horse, which is what the denial has to work against.
annotation.definitionFit: The whole clue defines it: the horse-shaped beast of legend known by the single spiralled horn on its brow, the one point that says it is no horse.

entries.clue: To the rear, somewhat different (5)

indicators.note: Somewhat means to some extent and no further, so only a stretch of what stands beside it is wanted.

blocks.note: the letters run consecutively out of the first word, through the whole of the second and into the third

annotation.surface: Something positioned at the back, and somewhat unlike the rest of them.
annotation.walkthrough: Three tiny words are a fine place to hide five letters, because the eye skims 'to the' without reading it at all. 'Somewhat' comes after its fodder, which is the only warning the clue gives.
annotation.definitionFit: different → OTHER: a thing other than the one in hand is a thing different from it, and the two adjectives swap straight over.

entries.clue: Sample taken from cover (duet), Not Before Time (7)

indicators.note: A sample is a small piece cut out of something larger, and that piece is what the clue is offering.

blocks.note: the letters run on consecutively from the tail of the first word into the bracketed one, the bracket no barrier at all

annotation.surface: A snatch sampled from somebody's cover version of a duet, for a track called Not Before Time.
annotation.walkthrough: The italics dress the last three words up as a track title, and they are the definition. A bracket and a word boundary are the only things standing between the answer and the eye.
annotation.definitionFit: Not Before Time → OVERDUE: the exclamation you make when a thing finally turns up later than it should have, which is what overdue describes.

entries.clue: Thirtieth: then go bananas or behave appropriately? (3,3,5,4)

indicators.note: Bananas is slang for out of your mind, and a word driven out of its mind will not keep its letters in line.

blocks.note: fifteen letters of fodder, the colon no obstacle

annotation.surface: A thirtieth birthday at which you either go wild or mind your manners.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Go bananas' reads as one phrase and the join runs right through it: 'go' is fodder, 'bananas' is the instruction. The definition is the sober alternative the clue offers instead.
annotation.definitionFit: behave appropriately → HIT THE RIGHT NOTE: the musician's idiom carried over to conduct, striking exactly the tone an occasion calls for.

entries.clue: Most important thing is vintage cross (4)

blocks.note: a cru is a French vineyard and the wine that comes off it, as in grand cru
the mark you put in a ballot box

annotation.surface: Something old and bad-tempered being called the thing that matters most.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cross' sits at the end of the sentence looking like the adjective for annoyed, and it is the pencil mark. The Latin for a cross is crux, so the wordplay is quietly telling you where the word came from.
annotation.definitionFit: Most important thing → CRUX: the crux of a matter is the point the whole of it hangs on, the knot that has to be untied before anything else moves.

entries.clue: A Freudian concept, to begin with, scarcely helps (4)

indicators.note: To begin with points at the start of a thing, so the word it governs gives up the letter it opens on.

blocks.note: the letter is handed over as itself
Freud's id is the unruly part of the mind, the one that simply wants things
the first letter of the word

annotation.surface: A psychoanalytic idea that from the outset is barely any use to anybody.
annotation.walkthrough: 'To begin with' is parked between the concept and the word it actually governs, which is what makes the last letter hard to place. Freud's id is standard crossword furniture and worth owning.
annotation.definitionFit: helps → AIDS: a plain synonym, to aid being to help, and both verbs taking the same s for their third person.
